stories.summary: We’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.

sources.name: Anthropic
sources.title: Investing in the public benefit
sources.text: Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline. As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company. The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them. We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad. Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit. This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones. In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report. To evaluate the safety of our systems, Anthropic is giving employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models, and we're in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face. Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms. Anthropic has opened an office in Singapore and signed an MOU with the country’s government to advance safe, responsible AI adoption.

stories.summary: Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI. Its security team investigates threats faster and proposes patches in minutes.

sources.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology
sources.text: Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work. Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter At Block, the company behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks. Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a new teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.” Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result. For example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming. The team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he says. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path. The automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim says, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.” Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years. In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy issue on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of issues. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James says. Another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes. Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the issue lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.” While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim says, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.” Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry. 18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises. Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back. Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter. 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations. Detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly. As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. sources.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
sources.text: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. stories.title: How to Use MiMo-V2.6 for Computer Vision with Roboflow
stories.summary: Try MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Playground for OCR, counting, and visual reasoning, then pair it with RF-DETR in Workflows for defect inspection.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Use MiMo-V2.6 for Computer Vision with Roboflow
sources.text: MiMo-V2.6 Flash does well on OCR, counting, and visual reasoning. You can test it in Roboflow Playground, then add it to a Workflow with the OpenRouter block. Roboflow Playground supports more than 130 vision models across 25 vision tasks, including MiMo-V2.6 Flash. In this article, I use Playground to test MiMo on several image-based tasks, then configure the same model in Roboflow Workflows . MiMo-V2.6 is Xiaomi's multimodal model family. It includes two variants: MiMo-V2.6 Pro and MiMo-V2.6 Flash . Both support text, images, video, and audio. Flash is the efficiency-focused version and is the main model tested in this article. For vision tasks, MiMo works differently from a dedicated detector. A detector is designed to return object classes and locations. MiMo can read visible text, describe image content, answer questions, and understand relationships in a scene. Choose MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Playground and select the task you want to run. For an OCR test, select OCR and upload the image. The model processes the image directly and returns the detected text. Playground lets you run the same task with different models and compare their results. The tests below focus on MiMo-V2.6 Flash. For questions that do not fit one of the available options, switch to Open Prompt. This mode lets you upload an image and write your own instruction. I used it for the counting test and the visual reasoning test, where the model needed to answer a specific question about the scene. I started with a simple OCR test using a bottle production image. The labels use large, front-facing text, with the lot code and expiry date clearly visible. MiMo-V2.6 Flash read the label correctly, including LOT 241015 and EXP 2025-10-30. For the second test, I used an industrial carton with smaller text, angled labels, barcodes, and glare on parts of the packaging. The model still captured the main label well. It read P/N: 142-7A305 correctly, along with the serial number and lot number. It also picked up the date, pressure range, output value, and the smaller technical text near the bottom of the label. The side label was partly captured. Its angle and partial view make some of the text unclear to check reliably. For that reason, this OCR test focused on text that could actually be read from the source image. For the next test, I switched to Open Prompt and used the same bottle production image. Prompt: How many bottles are visible on the conveyor? Briefly describe the production scene. MiMo-V2.6 Flash counted seven bottles, which matches the image. It also described the scene as an automated orange juice bottling line and recognized the conveyor setup. The response noticed that one bottle was uncapped while the others had caps. The scene description included one inaccurate assumption. MiMo suggested that the uncapped bottle was still in the capping stage. Since capped bottles appear on both sides of it, the image points more toward a missed capping step. The test showed that MiMo could count the bottles correctly and understand the production scene, though its explanation of the uncapped bottle needed closer checking. For the reasoning test, I kept the same production-line image and changed the question. This time, the prompt asked MiMo to find the bottle that broke the visual pattern in the row: Prompt: Which bottle breaks the visual pattern of the row? Give its position from the left and explain the visible difference. MiMo-V2.6 Flash correctly picked the fourth bottle from the left and identified the missing white cap as the difference. To answer the prompt, the model had to spot the anomaly and match it to a specific position in the row. The response matched what was visible in the image without adding another assumption about the production process. After testing MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Playground, the next step was to try the model in Roboflow Workflows with an inspection task . Playground provides a quick way to test MiMo across the available options and see how it handles different types of visual input. Workflows let the model run as part of a reusable pipeline and connect with other processing steps. For this Workflow test, a more challenging production-line image was used with more bottles and several packaging differences. The Workflow sends the image from the Inputs block to the OpenRouter block , then returns the result through the Outputs block. In the OpenRouter settings, the model is set to xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash, and the task type is Open Prompt. The prompt asks MiMo to inspect each bottle for visible packaging defects and flag any issues it finds. After running the Workflow, MiMo returned its inspection through the open_router_output field. MiMo flagged two bottles, correctly identifying the sixth from the left as missing its cap and the eighth as having a damaged label. The next bottle had a crooked cap, but MiMo did not flag it in this full-image run. The next Workflow adds an object detection step before MiMo so each bottle can be checked separately. RF-DETR Nano first detects the bottles in the production image, then a Dynamic Crop block creates one crop for each detection and passes those crops to MiMo-V2.6 Flash for inspection. With the bottles cropped, MiMo receives one bottle at a time. The prompt asks it to check the cap and label, then return the result in the same format for every crop: Status: PASS/FAIL | Cap: correct/missing/crooked/uncertain | Label: normal/wrinkled/torn/peeling/uncertain MiMo correctly flagged the bottle with the missing cap and the bottle with the wrinkled label; both results matched the visible defects in the image. The other bottle crops were returned as passes. The bottle with the crooked cap was still classified as “Cap: correct” after it was cropped. MiMo missed the same defect even with a closer view. sources.title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
sources.text: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models Authors Jie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of 0.798 across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with 0.776 for a CNN and 0.751 for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora. Olaussonâ¡**, Devon Hjelm, Paul Dixon, JoÃ£o Monteiro, Pierre Ablin, Vishnu Banna, Arno Blaas, Nick Henderson, Kari Noriy, Dan Busbridge, Josh Susskind, Marco Cuturi, Irina Belousova, Luca Zappella, Russ Webb, Jason RamapuramÂ§** Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based reparameterization, eliminating the need for tuning the optimal batch size as reported in recent work. This reparameterization decouples the physical batch size, often chosen based on compute (GPU saturation, FLOP-efficiency, wall-clock time) from the logical batch size, chosen to balance the variance of gradients during stochastic optimization. Finally, we pretrain a preliminary model showcasing the capabilities of a unified design, achieving strong results at 3B model scale (6.4T tokens), in both text generation, T2I tasks, and T2S tasks. Our work represents the largest scale systematic open study of multimodal discrete diffusion models conducted to date, providing valuable insights into scaling behaviors across multiple modalities. stories.title: What Are MCP Tools and How Do AI Models Use Them?
stories.summary: Learn what MCP tools are, how AI models discover and call them, and how to avoid common MCP tool problems.

sources.name: Perplexity
sources.title: What Are MCP Tools and How Do AI Models Use Them?
sources.text: Learn what MCP tools are, how AI models find and call them through MCP servers, and how to use them safely. MCP tools are functions an AI model can call to perform a task outside the conversation. For example, search your notes or query a database. Each tool sits on an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server and has a name and a short description that help the model decide when to use it. The term "MCP tool" is used in other ways too. In everyday use, people say "MCP tools" when they mean MCP servers (the applications that offer tools) or the directories that list those servers. MCP Tools is also the name of a command-line program for listing and calling the tools on an MCP server. This guide is about the protocol functions, not servers, directories, or command lines. It explains what a tool consists of, the kinds of tools servers offer, and how tools differ from resources, prompts, and function calling. It then walks through the steps a model takes to use a tool, and closes with the most common problems related to their use. An MCP tool is a function that lets AI models complete tasks with other software applications. For instance, my AI agents and workflows use MCP tools to draft emails in Gmail ( create_draft ), create Trello cards ( trelloWriteCard ), and pull live search results from DataForSEO ( serp_organic_live_advanced ), to name just a few. Software apps often offer multiple MCP tools on their MCP servers. For example, the Trello MCP server currently has 14 MCP tools that enable AI models to read and update boards, lists, checklists, cards, and more. And because MCP standardizes how tools are described and offered, any AI app that supports the protocol can use the same MCP tool. Some tools add extra metadata: a display name, a description of the results they return (an output schema), and annotations about how the tool behaves. The AI model never sees the code behind a tool. It works from what the tool says about itself, so a vague name or description leads the model to pick the wrong tool. MCP tools fall into four groups by what they do: Besides MCP tools, an MCP server can offer two other types of building blocks, which the protocol calls primitives: resources and prompts. For example, GitHub's official MCP server offers: The difference is what each one does and who decides when to use one: you, the AI app you're working in (e.g., Perplexity), or the AI model running inside that app. An AI model uses an MCP tool in five steps: discovery, tool selection, invocation, results, and error handling. Your AI app passes everything between the model and the server. Say you ask your AI app to check your Trello "This week" list and draft an email to your editor with an update. Here's what happens end to end: The key point is that the model chooses tools from their descriptions alone, and your AI app does all the talking to servers. Problems with MCP tools come down to four things: how many tools are connected, how they're named and described, how much data they return, and which servers they come from. Here's what each problem looks like and what helps: Every tool definition sits in the model's context window before you've asked anything, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Connect only the servers a task needs, and turn off unused tools where your AI app allows it. Example: GitHub's MCP server lets you enable only the groups of tools (toolsets) you need. The model calls the wrong tool, or the right one with the wrong inputs, because two descriptions sound alike or one says too little. Provide clear, specific names and descriptions, ideally with an example of when to use the tool. If a server's tools keep misfiring, MCP Inspector, the official testing tool, shows exactly what each tool says about itself. Two servers each offer a tool called search , and there's no telling which one a call is meant for. Prefix tool names with the server's name. Example: Trello's server ( trelloSearch , trelloReadList ). A tool returns more than the task needs, such as a whole email thread with its formatting, and crowds the model's context. Use tools that offer compact formats. Example: Gmail's get_thread tool description recommends plain-text format "to prevent context exhaustion." A careless or malicious server could use tool calls to pull data out of your conversation. Connect servers only from sources you trust, and keep approvals on for tools that change things or send data out. MCP tools need your approval because, without it, the AI model could make changes you didn't intend or share sensitive data with a server you don't control. A misread request or a vaguely described tool can trigger the wrong action. Every call also sends some of your information to a server. That's why the protocol expects AI apps to keep a person in the loop, with the ability to deny any tool call. Here's a practical way to sort tools by how much checking they need: Perplexity works with MCP tools in both directions: it can use tools from MCP servers you connect, and it offers its own tools to other AI apps. No, MCP isn't just tool calling. Tool calling is how the model asks for a tool, and MCP is how the AI app finds tools and routes each call to the server that runs it. Tool calling (also called function calling) is the AI model's part of the job: the model sees a list of tools and replies with a request to run one. With tool calling alone, each AI app has to define and run every tool itself. MCP lets tools live on servers, so any AI app that supports MCP can offer them to its model and send the model's requests to the right server. No, MCP won't replace APIs, because MCP and APIs work together. MCP tools often sit on top of existing APIs, and when the model calls a tool, the MCP server typically makes an API request. sources.title: How SPACE routes requests to the right sandbox execution
sources.text: Perplexity's SPACE binds AI agent requests to the right sandbox execution with identity checks and signed routes. When someone asks an AI agent to analyze a spreadsheet or test software, theyâre trusting it to work safely with their files and data. Agents need isolated environments where they can carry out that work without exposing other usersâ data or interfering with their workloads. As agents take on more complex tasks with greater autonomy, these environments help contain mistakes and limit the damage that unsafe or malicious code can cause. Sandboxes provide that isolation while sharing control-plane services, worker nodes, and routing infrastructure. That shared infrastructure must deliver each operation to the execution authorized to handle it. A stale route can send a valid request to another sandbox, or to an older execution of the right sandbox. SPACE , Perplexityâs secure sandbox platform, binds each operation to a selected execution and checks the destination before forwarding. For months, SPACE has handled millions of executions per day, each protected by a unique cryptographic identity, with an error rate below 0.0002% and zero dropped connections. Sandbox security also depends on getting each request to the right destination. Even a simple file read passes through shared infrastructure that must keep track of where the sandbox is running as it pauses, resumes, or moves between machines. A file read travels through several components. SPACEâs control plane resolves the sandbox to an execution and worker. The request enters through node-api , passes to the sandbox manager, sbx-manager , and crosses a Unix socket to the host bridge, spaced-host . The bridge forwards it over VSOCK, the host-to-guest socket transport, to spaced-guest inside the Firecracker microVM. Each decision relies on state that can lag behind infrastructure changes. A database may retain an old placement, a cached address may point elsewhere, or a socket path may acquire a different listener. A successful connection can still reach the wrong destination. A read could expose another userâs data; a write could modify the wrong filesystem. Snapshots add another issue. Resuming a sandbox on another worker preserves its logical identity but starts a new execution. A delayed request or surviving connection may reach its predecessor and return old state under the right sandbox name. SPACE separates the userâs environment from the runtime serving it: An execution generation distinguishes runtime incarnations. On Kubernetes, the route also includes the pod UID. Addresses locate endpoints; execution identity determines whether those endpoints may serve the operation. Suppose sandbox S runs as execution 7 on worker A, then resumes as execution 8 on worker B. A request selected for execution 8 must fail if it reaches execution 7. Checking only the sandbox ID would miss the disagreement. Each request carries signed proof of which sandbox execution may handle it and what access is allowed. The receiving component checks that proof against its own runtime identity before letting the request proceed. After caller authorization, SPACE issues a short-lived, signed capability identifying the sandbox, execution, placement, and permitted access. Public service-port capabilities also specify the allowed port and protocol. The receiving sandbox manager verifies the signature and compares the complete identity with its locally persisted runtime record. The signature establishes who authorized the selection. The comparison establishes whether that selection matches the receiver. ServicePort traffic receives a second check at the per-sandbox network gateway, netgtw , before a guest connection opens. The gateway compares the identity against trusted activation state and checks the port and protocol. Control operations proceed to bridge endpoint verification. SPACE uses Ed25519 signatures. Control-plane signing keys issue capabilities; public verification keys on workers and gateways cannot issue them. Capabilities last 120 seconds, with up to 15 seconds of expiration clock-skew allowance. A valid signature and unexpired token are still insufficient when the selected and installed identities disagree. The receiving worker can catch a routing mistake even when the request itself is authorized. It checks whether it is running the execution selected for that request and rejects the request if they differ. If a request selected for execution 8 reaches worker A, which still serves execution 7, worker A rejects it before forwarding. Once a receiver installs execution 8âs identity, it also rejects capabilities for execution 7, even before they expire. Thereâs an important boundary to this guarantee. A capability for execution 7 can still match a worker serving execution 7 until that worker learns of retirement or the capability expires. Local enforcement and bounded capability lifetime work together while updates propagate. A matching runtime record establishes the intended execution. The control bridge must also reach the processes and transport belonging to that activation, rather than a replacement that inherited the same address. The sandbox and node managers verify the host bridgeâs peer credentials and both bridge and Firecracker process identities, including start times, detecting reused IDs or changed executables Transport checks tie the VSOCK listener to the expected Firecracker process using socket ownership, guest identity, and kernel socket evidence. The bridge forwards operations only after verification and refuses transparent reconnects. Every new connection must pass the checks again. This verification covers the Firecracker control bridge on Kubernetes and directly managed hosts. ServicePort traffic uses execution and port checks at its gateway; it does not attest the identity of an arbitrary application inside the guest.
